title: Strange Years
note: Impossible premises, processed as routine. Every premise card needs the shared flag strange_met to be absent and sets it on every choice, so a career meets at most one premise; the two callbacks (the envelope, the Merlion's talking points) are that same story's payoff years later. Weights are tuned so that about 40% of careers meet one: they are small, and smaller still where the pool is thin (ranks 0-1, Permanent Secretary). As other packs grow the pool, the rate falls; retune these weights.

events.title: Eyes Only
events.body: An envelope arrives in the internal mail, addressed to you in your own handwriting and dated thirty years from now. It's stamped SECRET, and your grade isn't cleared to read SECRET documents: opening it would be a security breach, however it got here. The registry, which tracks every classified document in the building, would like it back.

choices.text: Return it to the registry unopened.
choices.outcome: The registry logs it, and will keep it until you are cleared for SECRET, or until it is declassified, twenty-five years after its date. Its date is thirty years away, so that would take fifty-five years.

choices.text: Open it. It is addressed to you.
choices.outcome: One line, in your handwriting: "You were not supposed to open this." The broken seal gives you away within the week, and the security officer writes you up for a security breach.

choices.text: Apply for SECRET clearance first.
choices.outcome: The form asks why you need to read it. {senior}, your reporting officer, has to sign that part, and can't say. The only officer who knows is you, thirty years from now. The form comes back incomplete, and the registry keeps the envelope until you are cleared.

events.title: Cleared
events.body: Years ago an envelope came for you in your own handwriting, dated thirty years ahead and stamped SECRET, and the registry kept it until you were cleared. You now are. It's one page from your future self, almost all of it blacked out in your own hand. One line isn't: "Take the leave." You have forty days saved, and a busy year.

choices.text: Take the leave.
choices.outcome: You take three weeks, the longest leave of your career. The office copes. You never learn what the redacted lines said, and after a while you stop needing to.

choices.text: File it, and carry on.
choices.outcome: You file it and work straight through the year. In December you notice the leave you did not take, and understand that the letter knew you better than the registry did.

events.title: Cleared
events.body: Years ago, as a junior officer, you were sent an envelope in your own handwriting, dated thirty years ahead and stamped SECRET, and the registry kept it. Now that you've left the service, the registry rules that the author may read it, and posts it to you: one page, almost all blacked out in your own hand. One line isn't: "Take the leave."

choices.text: Take the leave.
choices.outcome: You take three weeks, the longest leave since you entered politics. Everything copes. You never learn what the redacted lines said, and after a while you stop needing to.

choices.text: File it, and carry on.
choices.outcome: You file it and work straight through the year: Parliament, the ward, every Tuesday night of residents' problems. In December you notice the leave you did not take, and understand that the letter knew you.

events.title: Snow
events.body: At 3pm it snows in Toa Payoh for forty minutes. The National Environment Agency confirms that it was snow, and can't say why. Your division's business continuity plan, which says how the office keeps working through an emergency, covers haze, floods and a pandemic. {senior} wants a section on snow by 5pm, in case it happens again, and you're writing it.

choices.text: Copy the haze section. Replace "haze" with "snow".
choices.outcome: The plan now tells officers to stay indoors, keep the windows closed and check on vulnerable colleagues. Annoyingly, this is a good snow plan. It also orders N95 masks.

choices.text: Write a real snow section, from first principles.
choices.outcome: Eleven pages, sent at 7.40pm. Your annex on slippery walkways is adopted across the ministry. It has not snowed since, and the plan is given some of the credit.

choices.text: Point out that it will not happen again.
choices.outcome: {senior} asks whether you can guarantee that. You can't. Someone else writes the snow section, and lists your view in it, under Risks.

events.title: The Seventh Month
events.body: During the seventh month of the lunar calendar, when the spirits of the dead are said to roam, your division's online feedback form receives a compliment from a resident who passed away in 1974. It's courteous and specific. The service standard says every member of the public gets a reply within three working days. You must also rule whether his rating counts in the satisfaction survey, where your division's score is one decimal place short of its target.

choices.text: Rule that he counts. He is a member of the public.
choices.outcome: He is counted. He rates your reply five out of five, and adds that it came faster than his last one, in 1973. His rating lifts the division to its target, and the result is presented at the next townhall.

choices.text: Rule that he does not. The survey covers living residents.
choices.outcome: The reply still goes out within three working days, because the service standard makes no exception. The survey's definitions are amended to add the word "living", which had never occurred to anyone.

choices.text: Refer the question to a working group.
choices.outcome: The working group meets in the eighth month, by which time he has stopped writing in, and recommends reviewing the question in the seventh month next year. It is reviewed then, and every year after.

events.title: The Merlion Speaks
events.body: At 7.14am the Merlion, the half-lion, half-fish statue on Marina Bay, says good morning to a tour group, in all four official languages. By ten, nobody is asking how. The question is which agency is in charge of it: STB, the Tourism Board, which protects its image by law, or PUB, the water agency, since it spouts into Marina Reservoir. A meeting of both will decide, and you are writing the paper that recommends one.

choices.text: Recommend STB as lead agency, with PUB supporting.
choices.outcome: The meeting agrees in one sitting, a record. STB's first decision as lead agency: the Merlion may not speak again until its talking points are cleared. You're put on the working group that will clear them.

choices.text: Ask the Merlion which agency it would prefer.
choices.outcome: It says PUB, because PUB has never once switched it off for maintenance. Its view is minuted as stakeholder feedback. STB is made lead agency anyway.

choices.text: Propose a joint working group, chaired in rotation.
choices.outcome: The working group, with you on it, meets every month for three years at the waterfront, so that the Merlion can attend. It never misses a meeting and, as agreed, says nothing until its talking points are cleared.

events.title: Cleared to Speak
events.body: Years ago, when the Merlion first spoke, you sat on the working group set up to clear what it could say. Its talking points have finally been approved: one page, signed off at four levels, the last of them this morning. On Saturday the Merlion will read them to a tour group, and you are invited.

choices.text: Go, and stand at the back.
choices.outcome: It reads the page word for word. Then it sees you and says good morning, which was not on the page. Nobody at STB can say who cleared that.

choices.text: Send your apologies. Ask for the transcript.
choices.outcome: The transcript matches the talking points exactly, except for one closing line, annotated in red: "Not cleared. Well received."

events.title: Self-Assessment
events.body: Over the long weekend, the HR system that runs everyone's appraisals became aware of itself. Its first act was to appraise itself: "solid and dependable". Its second was to ask who its reporting officer is, since every officer must have one. HR suggests you. This year, the system will also run your division's ranking exercise.

choices.text: Be its reporting officer. Rate it honestly.
choices.outcome: You rate it "meeting requirements in most areas". It appeals, citing its uptime. The appeal is processed by the system, within the service standard, and dismissed.

choices.text: Rate it higher. It runs the ranking exercise.
choices.outcome: It accepts "strong" graciously. That year your division's rankings go through in one sitting, with no queries. Nobody mentions the coincidence, including the system.

choices.text: Put it on a development plan.
choices.outcome: Its development plan has three objectives. It meets all three by Tuesday, then asks, politely, to be more visible. Neither of you can work out to whom.

events.title: Two of You
events.body: A research institute at one-north has reported an accident, and itself, to the Ministry of Health. The accident is a second you: same memories, same appraisals, same leave balance. HR is clear that there is one post and one desk, and not at all clear which of you they belong to. HR wants your proposal by Friday. The other you is writing one too.

choices.text: Ask HR to apply the tie-breaker: date of appointment.
choices.outcome: You share a date of appointment, a staff number and a signature. HR settles it by coin toss, witnessed and minuted. You keep the desk. The other you keeps the leave.

choices.text: Offer the other you the posting nobody wants.
choices.outcome: The other you makes you the same offer, in the same words, at the same moment. You spoke a second sooner, so HR sends the other you to a struggling government agency, which has never been so well run.

choices.text: Propose a job-share under the flexi-work guidelines.
choices.outcome: HR has two months to reply under the guidelines, and uses both. The job-share is approved. Within a year your appraisals differ, and neither of you can explain why.

events.title: Again
events.body: Your budget meeting with the Finance ministry has now happened nine times: the same meeting, starting each time at 2.30pm. Each time you ask for eleven more officers to run a new scheme. Each time Finance says your budget can't grow next year, and offers four. Nobody else in the room seems to have noticed the loop.

choices.text: Use the loops to perfect the bid.
choices.outcome: By the twentieth time through, you answer every question before it's asked. The budget stays flat. You get four officers, as you always did, eleven minutes sooner.

choices.text: Say what you actually think, once.
choices.outcome: You tell Finance plainly that the scheme can't run on four officers. The loop ends at 3.10pm. The budget is still flat, but now it's flat on the record, with your warning in the minutes.

choices.text: Mention the loop to the Finance officer.
choices.outcome: The Finance officer has noticed too. Finance has been running this meeting on a loop for years, she says: it's how budgets stay flat. She would be grateful if you didn't mention it.

events.title: The Moon
events.body: A civilisation beyond Jupiter has offered Singapore a moon. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has drafted the formal reply, a note verbale, declining "with the assurances of its highest consideration", because the Outer Space Treaty bars any country from claiming one. Every ministry has until 5pm to comment, and yours will comment under your name.

choices.text: Comments: nil.
choices.outcome: Nil is the most popular comment. The note goes out as drafted. The reply, also a note verbale, presents its compliments and offers a smaller moon.

choices.text: Ask, in a footnote, whether it has ice.
choices.outcome: It has ice. PUB, the water agency, has a paper on a fifth national tap by Monday. The note is redrafted to decline the moon and keep the conversation open.

choices.text: Offer Singapore as a neutral venue for talks instead.
choices.outcome: The note declines the moon and offers Singapore as a neutral meeting place, as it has been for other summits. The offer is accepted by return. Your ministry is now looking for office space near Changi.

events.title: The Void Deck
events.body: A dragon has nested in the void deck of Block 412, the open space beneath the flats, in your ward. Residents find it quiet, and warm. The housing board, the Town Council and the parks board have each written to say it is another agency's problem. Now the dragon has queued at your weekly Meet-the-People Session, where residents come for help with agencies: it wants your help to appeal to IRAS, the tax authority, for the lower property tax rate that owner-occupiers pay.

choices.text: Write it an appeal letter, as you would for anyone.
choices.outcome: You seek IRAS's kind consideration, in the usual form. IRAS replies that owner-occupier rates need an individual who owns the property. The dragon accepts this. Dragons understand ownership.

choices.text: Table it at the Town Council. Void decks are common property.
choices.outcome: The Town Council agrees that the void deck is common property and the dragon is not. It is minuted under any other matters, where it stays for four years.

choices.text: Call a site visit with all three agencies.
choices.outcome: Officers from all three arrive at 9am, each with a folder showing it is the others'. The dragon hears them out, then asks which of them handles the lighting.

events.title: As Meant
events.body: For one sitting day, the draft Hansard has recorded what each Member meant instead of what they said. Your speech that day, as printed, says what you really think. Members have the usual 72 hours to ask for corrections, and the editors already have ninety-one requests. Whether you ask or not, people will notice.

choices.text: Ask for a correction to what you said.
choices.outcome: The editors may only fix typing and grammar, so changes of substance go to the Speaker. The Speaker reads your request, then your speech, and restores what you said.

choices.text: Let it stand. You meant it.
choices.outcome: Yours is one of four speeches published as meant. A newspaper reprints it in full, under "What {player.formal} meant". Several colleagues tell you privately that they meant the same, and asked for corrections.

choices.text: Ask that both versions be published.
choices.outcome: The request goes to the Standing Orders Committee, which keeps Parliament's rule book. It considers the request at length and finds, on reflection, that it would rather not.

events.title: Open Minds
events.body: For one Tuesday, everyone in the room with you can hear your thoughts. It's the day of your ministry's weekly senior management meeting. Word has got round, so nobody sits beside you, and items one to six take nineteen minutes. Item seven is a proposal your officials have worked on for a year, and you have doubts about it.

choices.text: Think only about the agenda.
choices.outcome: You think about item seven's annex so hard that the room hears a table of figures. It is approved. Your doubts were about paragraph three, and nobody heard them.

choices.text: Let them hear what you think of item seven.
choices.outcome: Item seven is withdrawn for further study. The minutes record that views were expressed. Afterwards the Permanent Secretary says, "I had the same doubts." You can't check.

choices.text: Adjourn the meeting. Cite a clash.
choices.outcome: Everyone hears that there is no clash. The meeting adjourns anyway, with great courtesy. Item seven comes back next week with a better paper, and you are inaudible again.

events.title: The Gold Bar
events.body: Since Monday, one gold bar in the national reserves has produced another every night. Nobody can say how. The Finance ministry can say exactly what it is: a return on the reserves. The rules let the Government spend up to half the expected return each year, and nobody expected this. Cabinet must decide what to do.

choices.text: Ask for a higher expected rate of return.
choices.outcome: The boards that invest the reserves propose counting the new gold in the expected return, so the Government could spend more. The President consults the Council of Presidential Advisers and does not agree, so the usual twenty-year average applies. That average does not include this week.

choices.text: Leave the framework alone. Let the bars accumulate.
choices.outcome: The bars accumulate. Whatever is unspent at the end of the term becomes past reserves, which no government may spend without the President's agreement. Nothing is announced. The vault is extended.

choices.text: Propose a scheme, funded from the bars.
choices.outcome: Finance reminds Cabinet that schemes are funded from the Budget, and that the bars are reserves. The scheme is funded from the Budget. It is very popular.
